info.name: E-commerce Order Management
info.description:
Multi-warehouse order management: catalog, cart, checkout with reservation-based inventory, payments, fulfillment, returns and refunds.

## Setup

1. Start the app: `mvn spring-boot:run`
2. Run **1. Authentication → Login (customer)** — the token is captured automatically into a collection variable.
3. Work through the folders in order. Order ids, shipment ids, and return ids are all captured by test scripts, so nothing needs pasting by hand.

Collection-level Bearer auth is configured, so every request inherits the right token.

## Folders

| Folder | What it demonstrates |
|---|---|
| 1. Authentication | Login for each role |
| 2. Catalog (public) | Browse without a token |
| 3. Cart & Pricing | The preview breakdown — discount cap, post-discount tax |
| 4. Checkout | Happy path, plus every payment failure branch |
| 5. Orders | Tracking, cancellation |
| 6. Fulfillment | Pack → ship → deliver as warehouse staff |
| 7. Returns & Refunds | Partial return with exact pro-rata refund |
| 8. Inventory (admin) | Stock levels, the movement ledger |
| 9. Admin — Catalog & Pricing | Products, coupons, tax rates |
| 10. Admin — Operations | Outbox health, audit trail, payment reconciliation |
| 11. Access Control | 403 by role, 404 for cross-customer |

## Seeded accounts

All with password `Password@123`: `admin@oms.dev`, `customer@oms.dev`, `customer2@oms.dev`, `staff.mum@oms.dev` (Mumbai), `staff.del@oms.dev` (Delhi).

## Forcing payment outcomes

The simulated gateway is deterministic. Set `paymentToken` to `tok_decline` (402), `tok_timeout` (502, holds retained), `tok_error` (502), `tok_slow` (slow success), or anything else (success).

item.name: 1. Authentication
item.description: Tokens are captured into collection variables by the test scripts.

request.description: Stateless HS256 token, 12-hour TTL. Roles and warehouse assignment travel as claims, so request authorization needs no database round trip.
`warehouseIds` in the response is what scopes the fulfillment queue. Mumbai staff cannot act on a Delhi parcel.
Used by the access-control folder to prove cross-customer reads return 404.
Always yields ROLE_CUSTOMER. Letting a caller pick their role would make RBAC decorative.

item.name: 2. Catalog (public)
item.description: Unauthenticated on purpose: a storefront must be shoppable before anyone signs in.

request.description: Nested. The tree is not decoration: tax resolution walks it upward and browse walks it downward.
All filters optional and composable. Filtering by a parent category includes its descendants, so `categorySlug=apparel` also returns Men and Women products.
The `variants[].id` values here are what POST /cart/items expects.

item.name: 3. Cart & Pricing
item.description: The cart holds no prices and reserves no stock. Prices resolve from the live catalog; reservation begins at checkout.

request.description: Merges with an existing line for the same SKU rather than creating a duplicate.
Indicative subtotal only — call /cart/preview for the real breakdown. No endpoint accepts a cart id, so reading someone else's basket is unexpressible.

**The most informative call in the collection.** Runs the same pricing engine checkout runs, so the preview cannot disagree with the charge.

| | Amount | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Subtotal | 15998.00 | 2 × 7999.00 |
| Discount | 500.00 | SAVE10 is 10% (1599.80) but **caps at 500.00** |
| Tax | 2789.64 | 18% of **15498.00** — the *post-discount* base |
| Shipping | 0.00 | free above 999.00 post-discount |
| **Total** | **18287.64** | |

Also note `lines[0].lineDiscount` — the coupon apportioned down to the line. That is persisted on the order at checkout, and is what makes a correct partial refund computable later.
An invalid coupon fails loudly with the reason rather than being silently ignored — otherwise the customer stares at a total that does not match the promotion they were shown.
Absolute value, not a delta.

item.name: 4. Checkout
item.description:
The one endpoint that runs a saga:

```
TX-1   reserve · price · persist order+payment      locks held, ms
——     gateway call                    NO transaction, NO locks
TX-2   commit+capture  OR  release+fail             locks held, ms
——     outbox: routing · notification · audit   after the response
```

exec: // A fresh key per run, so the request is not replayed from a previous run.
pm.test('charged total equals the previewed total', () => pm.expect(Number(d.grandTotal.amount)).to.eql(18287.64));
pm.test('routed to at least one warehouse', () => pm.expect(d.fulfillingWarehouseIds).to.not.be.empty);

header.description: Required. A UUID or any unique string.

request.description:
Run **3. Cart → Add 2 x Nimbus Buds Pro** first.

The response total is *exactly* the previewed total, because both run one pricing engine.

`zone: WEST` is the allocation proximity hint — it makes the strategy prefer the Mumbai warehouse.

Fulfillment routing, the notification, and the audit trail all run **after** this response.

exec: pm.test('same order, not a new one', () => pm.expect(String(pm.response.json().data.orderId)).to.eql(String(pm.collectionVariables.get('orderId'))));

request.description:
Send immediately after the previous request — identical key, identical body.

Same order id, same 201, `Idempotent-Replay: true`, and **one** charge. No second order and no second unit of stock consumed. This is the guard against a double-clicked Pay button.
Replaying here would hand the caller an answer to a question they did not ask, which is worse than an error.

Add an item to the cart first.

A decline is **final**, so the stock hold goes straight back. The order is kept as `PAYMENT_FAILED` rather than deleted, so the customer sees the attempt in their history and support can explain it.

exec: pm.test('client told the retry is safe', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().details[0].retrySafe).to.be.true);

request.description:
**The most interesting failure branch.** The gateway gave no answer, so the charge may or may not have happened.

The stock hold is deliberately **retained** — releasing it could sell units the customer has already paid for. The payment is flagged `UNCONFIRMED` and appears in **10. Admin → Unconfirmed payments**.

If nothing resolves it, the reservation TTL returns the stock and the sweeper cancels the order. Bounded and self-healing rather than permanently inconsistent.

First add **3** units of variant 9 (`TEE-BLK-M`) to the cart — it is seeded with exactly **one** unit network-wide.

The error carries a per-SKU shortfall so the client can tell the customer exactly which line failed and by how much. Nothing is held: TX-1 rolled back entirely.

For the real proof — 50 simultaneous checkouts against that one unit — run:
`mvn verify -Dit.test=OversellPreventionIT -Dtest=MoneyTest`
Scoped to the authenticated customer.
Money breakdown, per-line discount share and tax, payment state, `refundedTotal`, and `allowedNextStatuses` read straight from the state machine — so a client never hard-codes the lifecycle.
The form a customer reads off a confirmation.

Permitted from `AWAITING_PAYMENT`, `CONFIRMED`, `PACKED`. Once `SHIPPED`, returns 409 — the goods are with a carrier and returns are the only route back.

One transaction, **refund before restock**: if the refund fails everything rolls back. Also releases the coupon redemption.

item.name: 6. Fulfillment
item.description: Warehouse staff. Uses `{{staffToken}}` — run **1. Authentication → Login (warehouse staff)** first.

request.description: Scoped to the warehouses this staff member is assigned to. These shipments were created by the **asynchronous** pipeline, so a queue entry is itself evidence that routing ran after the checkout response.

exec: pm.test('at least one parcel exists', () => pm.expect(shipments).to.not.be.empty);

request.description: A split allocation produces more than one parcel, each moving independently.
The **order** status is derived from the least advanced parcel, so a two-parcel order only becomes PACKED once both are packed.
Starts the return window, which is measured from **delivery** — a parcel that took two weeks to arrive should not eat the customer's return period.
Send after DELIVERED. The transition table is closed by default, and the message names what *is* allowed.

item.name: 7. Returns & Refunds
item.description: A customer may **ask**; only staff or an admin may **approve**. Letting the requester approve would mean self-service refunds with no inspection of the goods.

exec: pm.test('line carries its apportioned discount share', () => pm.expect(line).to.have.property('lineDiscount'));

request.description: Captures `orderLineId` for the next request.

exec: pm.test('awaiting review — nothing refunded yet', () => pm.expect(d.status).to.eql('REQUESTED'));
pm.test('refund is half of what was PAID (9143.82), not half the list price (7999)', () => pm.expect(Number(d.totalRefund.amount)).to.eql(9143.82));

request.description:
Requires the order to be `DELIVERED` — run folder 6 first.

**The refund figure is the point.** Returning 1 of 2 units refunds `9143.82` — half of the `18287.64` actually *paid*, with the discount share and tax both reversed. Half the list price would be `7999.00`, which would under-refund the tax and over-refund the discount.

Quantities are validated against what is still returnable, counting approved **and pending** claims, so two pending requests cannot together return more than was bought.

Try `reason: "DAMAGED"` to see `restockable: false` — damaged goods are refunded but deliberately not restocked, because putting them back would promise a unit that cannot ship.

One transaction, **refund first**: if the gateway refuses, everything rolls back and the request stays `REQUESTED` for a retry. Restocking first and then failing to refund would leave the customer out of pocket with their goods already resold.

Goods go back to the warehouse that actually shipped them, keeping the shelf and the allocation strategy's proximity data in agreement.

The order becomes `RETURNED` if every unit has come back, otherwise `DELIVERED` so the remainder stays returnable.
Nothing refunded or restocked. The order returns to `DELIVERED` so the customer can raise a fresh request rather than being permanently stuck.

item.name: 8. Inventory (admin & staff)
item.description: Uses `{{adminToken}}`. Customers deliberately have no access: exact stock counts are competitive intelligence.

exec: pm.test('available is derived, never stored', () => pm.expect(d.totalAvailable).to.eql(d.totalOnHand - d.totalReserved));

request.description:
Variant 9 (`TEE-BLK-M`) is seeded with exactly **one** unit network-wide — 1 at Mumbai, 0 at Delhi. That is the oversell demo SKU.

`available` is always derived as `on_hand - reserved`. A stored availability column would be a second source of truth that drifts under concurrency, and the drift *is* the oversell.

Refused with 422 if the new level is below units already reserved for open orders — those belong to customers with confirmed orders, and silently invalidating them would trade a visible error for an invisible one.
Safe to apply concurrently with another adjustment, unlike an absolute set — two people each setting the level from a stale reading would lose one of the changes.

Append-only: every reserve, release, expiry, sale, restock, and adjustment, each recording the resulting `onHandAfter` and `reservedAfter`. This is how a stock discrepancy is bisected to the movement that caused it.
Re-parenting a category under its own descendant is refused. Deleting one with children or products is refused with 422 rather than cascading and orphaning rows.

item.name: Create a product with a variant

request.description:
The variant is the priced, stocked unit, which is why inventory keys on variant rather than product.

DELETE archives rather than removing: order lines still dereference the variant for returns and reporting.
Admin-only. Customers apply a coupon by code but can never enumerate the table, which would hand out every unadvertised promotion.

body.raw:
{
  "code": "WELCOME15",
  "description": "15% off your first order, capped at Rs.750",
  "type": "PERCENTAGE_OFF",
  "discountValue": 15.0,
  "maxDiscount": 750.00,
  "minOrderValue": 999.00,
  "startsAt": "2026-01-01T00:00:00Z",
  "endsAt": "2027-01-01T00:00:00Z",
  "usageLimit": 1000,
  "perCustomerLimit": 1
}

request.description:
`PERCENTAGE_OFF` (`discountValue` is a percentage, optionally capped) or `FLAT_AMOUNT_OFF` (an absolute amount, clamped to the basket so a total can never go negative).

Set `categoryId` to restrict to that category **and its descendants**. One coupon per order — stacking is out of scope and enforced by a unique constraint.

Sparse by design. Only Electronics (0.18), Apparel (0.05), and Home (0.12) have rows; Mobiles, Audio, Men, and Women **inherit** by walking the tree upward. A new sub-category is taxed correctly the moment it is created.

`rate` is a **fraction**: 0.28 means 28%. Rates are never percentages, so no division by one hundred appears anywhere in the pricing code.

Upsert, because a category has at most one rate.

item.name: 10. Admin — Operations
item.description: Production observability is out of scope; this is the minimum that makes the async design defensible, because an outbox silently accumulating dead letters is worse than no outbox at all.

request.description: Counts by status plus the registered handlers: `fulfillment-routing`, `customer-notification`, `audit-trail`. A non-zero `deadLetter` count is the signal that downstream work has been abandoned and needs a human.
Each row carries `attempts` and `lastError`, naming the handler that failed. A poison event is visible here rather than silently discarded.

Re-runs only the handlers that have not yet succeeded. Handlers that already completed are skipped via the `(event, handler)` execution marker, so redelivery cannot duplicate a notification or a shipment.

Every status change, cancellation, and return, newest first.

Each row carries the `traceId` of the request that caused it — **including rows written asynchronously minutes later**, because MDC is propagated across the thread hand-off. An audit entry therefore leads straight to the full log context.

The queue an operator checks against the provider's records after a gateway timeout. Run **4. Checkout → unknown outcome** first to populate it.

In a production build this is where a webhook or reconciliation job would settle these rows.
Filter by `status=AWAITING_PAYMENT` to spot checkouts that never settled.

item.name: 11. Access Control
item.description: Two distinct concerns, which fail in different ways: **role** checks return 403; **ownership** checks return **404**, because a 403 confirms the resource exists and enables enumeration.

request.description: Staff cannot shop.

exec: pm.test('200 — needed to pick an order', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));
pm.test('403 — staff could otherwise manufacture availability', () => pm.response.to.have.status(403));
pm.test('same error contract as everything else', () => {
pm.test('X-Trace-Id header present even on filter-chain failures', () => pm.expect(pm.response.headers.get('X-Trace-Id')).to.not.be.empty);
pm.test('NOT_FOUND — does not confirm the order exists', () => pm.expect(pm.response.json().code).to.eql('NOT_FOUND'));

request.description:
Run **1. Authentication → Login (second customer)** first.

**This is the check a role-only security model gets wrong**, and it is the most common data leak in commerce APIs. Ownership is enforced *in the query*, so a future caller cannot forget it, and the response deliberately does not distinguish "not yours" from "does not exist".

item.name: Login failures do not leak account existence

request.description: Unknown email and wrong password return an identical response. Distinguishing them would turn the endpoint into an account enumeration oracle.
